subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-70
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie):
That, in relation to Bill C-70, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, one sitting day be allotted to the consideration of the report stage of the said Bill and one further sitting day be allotted to the consideration of the Bill at the third reading stage; and
That 15 minutes before the expiry of the time provided for the consideration of government business on the above-mentioned sitting days, any proceedings then before the House shall be interrupted, if necessary, for the purpose of this Order and, in turn, every question necessary to dispose of the said stage of the said Bill shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, what we have before the House today is an approach by the Government to bring order to legislation which has had much debate at all stages that have been brought forward to date. First, the Bill before us had exposure in the Budget. In the budget debate, as all Hon. Members know, topics can be debated; it is a very wide-ranging debate and there is very minimal limitation, if in fact any exists, to debate the issues of the Budget and the economic affairs of the country.
There was a six-day debate in which, the Budget being the main motion, with amendments moved by the Official Opposition and by the NDP, the House disposed of not only the main motion but of every amendment and every sub-amendment.

When the Bill was being read the second time, again there was a division in the House and again the House decided, very clearly and in a wide majority view, that the Bill should be passed at second reading and passed in principle.
The Government did not stop there. This Bill was one of the first Bills which was subjected to the new House rules, namely reference to legislative committees. Under the rules on legislative committees, as all Hon. Members know, the size of the committee is generally much larger than that of standing committees. That Bill went through rigorous examination in committee.
Let us look at the British experience. When a Government or a Parliament has decided in principle on a Bill, then a legislative committee-and that is what its role is in the British parliamentary system-examines the principles of the Bill but, more important, examines it from the point of view of technicalities. This Government went further than that. Not only did we look at clauses, amendments and technicalities, we also asked witnesses from various groups in Canada to come forward. They made their points of view. That was also done, quite apart from what legislative committees had been established for in the British parliamentary system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians who are listening will now understand why most people call him the Minister of social injustice.
Mr. Speaker, this Minister has yet to understand what his role is supposed to be.
I think we should recall that in this country's history, whenever a Budget was brought down, every Minister of National Health and Welfare, and even the Conservative Minister of National Health and Welfare, and even the Conservative Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) who is here in the House, has seen it as his duty to defend the interests of the elderly, the sick and our families. This is the first time in Canada's history, under any government, that we have a Minister who is supposed to defend the interests of these people and who sees it as part of his ministerial duties to crush those very same people and take away their purchasing power.
Today he agreed to move a motion to impose closure on the Opposition. Mr. Speaker, if anyone asks us why the Members of the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party are violently opposed to this Bill, our answer is quite simply that the people of this country have asked us to do so.
The Minister has tried to show us how to behave with parliamentary hypocrisy, but I refuse to play the kind of game he wants to play in the House. The people of Montreal-Sainte-Marie did not elect and re-elect me to indulge in parliamentary hypocrisy; they elected me not to defend our institutions but to defend the interests of Canadian citizens.
Mr. Speaker, the role of Members in this House is not just to consider the British system or Canada, but to consider the people who live in this country.
Mr. Speaker, what this motion means, and I find this absolutely shocking, is that the Minister is asking us to cease debate at a time when Canadians, and I have a copy of the telegram sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and not only women are opposed to this measure, not just family agencies but the bishops as well, who are asking for a meeting with the Prime Minister on Friday . . . Mr. Speaker, these are the people who are asking their Members to object to the decision made by this Minister and by the Prime Minister.
We have received petitions from every riding in Canada, Mr. Speaker. Even people from the riding of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, even people from the Prime Minister's riding are against that measure.
And why are they, Mr. Speaker? First of all, because the Government wants to treat families the same way it tried to treat the elderly. They have been betrayed. People are angry with this Government, and angry with the Prime Minister because they have been misled.
Mr. Speaker, all this will go down in history. Remember when Mrs. Denis came up and told the Prime Minister in no uncertain terms: "You lied to us, Charlie Brown." She was right, and our Canadian mothers are saying the same thing. Mr. Speaker, this is the same Minister who bragged about consulting the people. This is the same Minister who, on behalf

of the Government, made a commitment to these people in a document bearing his signature, a document that says that any savings which may result from program changes will not be applied to a reduction of the deficit. That was to mislead the people and the organizations that came to testify. They thought they could trust him, but the Budget has proved them to be wrong.
Mr. Speaker, what the Minister then tried to have us believe about the new legislative committees was a lot of nonsense. First of all, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Members who were there were totally useless. All they tried to do was to obstruct debate, and all they wanted to do was leave. They did not even want to hear witnesses. The Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party had to force Government Members to listen to people who wanted to have their say. Extraordinary steps had to be taken to force the Government to hear the witnesses.
Still with respect to another Bill C-70 clause which has nothing to do with the de-indexation of family allowances, the Minister wanted full authority to decide on his own whether a missing child would be presumed dead. One outrageous incident was the case of a Quebec woman who came all the way to Ottawa. The Government could not spare any money to help her, but it is not so niggardly when time comes to throw a party. I was the one who found the money to bring this mother here to testify. I offered to give up my ten minutes just so she might give evidence before the committee, but the eleven Conservative Members turned me down right in front of the media.
The Minister is going too far, openly misleading the people, and that is why all Quebecers and all Canadians are fuming mad, Mr. Speaker. No wonder this morning's polls reveal that the popularity of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is going down fast. No wonder most Canadians are against the policies of this Government.
Mr. Speaker, we in the Official Opposition laid our cards on the table right after the Budget was introduced because we knew for a fact that three of its measures were unfair and unacceptable.
First, the de-indexation of old age security pensions. With the strong support of elderly Canadians we managed to make the Minister and all Conservative Members eat humble pie, and even the Prime Minister had to backtrack.
Second, the shameful tax on the health of citizens intended to enable the Government to recoup some money. Here again, in August, we were successful in throwing the Government off course, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Prime Minister and all the silent Conservative Members had to eat crow. The Government had no choice but to retreat.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that our fight for family allowances is not over, and we intend to use every means at our disposal.
Today the Minister announced a 4 per cent increase in Canada Pension Plan and old age security pension benefits.

Thanks to whom? Not thanks to the Conservative Government, but thanks to elderly Canadians who won their point. And then the Government has been unwilling to say by how much the family allowances cheques would increase. Canadians ought to know that if the Bill is adopted, monthly family allowances will go up by 37 cents in English Canada, and 18 cents for each child in Quebec.
Yesterday I listened to the Prime Minister on the Radio-Canada program "Le Point" when he kept repeating that he wanted to be generous with the people. Generous to the tune of 18 cents a month, big deal! At the same time the Government drops the guillotine to push through a Bill to bail out rich depositors who had over $60,000 in the western banks.
Mr. Speaker, you should not wonder . . . Which province does the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) come from? Which region is he from? Whose interests is he trying to defend, Mr. Speaker? His western Canadian chums who had money in the bank that went belly up because they were bad administrators, but he simply could not care less about the three million needy Canadian families.
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking to all the Conservative Members of Parliament, even those who are not in the House today, since it is useless to speak to the Minister as he is a lost cause. If you do not take steps in each of your constituencies to stop this Bill from being approved, if you do not take steps to ensure that family allowances will be fully indexed, if you continue to grovel before the Prime Minister, if you continue to be so spineless, if you continue to grovel and to defend the wealthy as you are now doing, during the coming months and next year, people will go to see you at your offices and ask you to justify yourselves.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, 1 would like to say that 1988 will come quickly, and during the next electoral campaign, the Conservative Members will do door-to-door canvassing, they will go to meetings, they will go and see the senior citizens and say that they need their support. The senior citizens will reply: "Where were you when I needed you? You did not take care of me; that's it!" As for families with children, when these Conservative Members go and see the mothers to tell them that they need them, they will say: "Where were you when it was time to defend our interests? You were not there so we are getting rid of you!" The same thing has been happening on all the issues, but I see that my alloted time is over. 1 urge the Conservative Members to reflect on this. It is Christmas time, the time of family reunions. It is the most important family holiday of the year, and I trust that the gift that the Prime Minister brings to Canadian men and women on New Year's day will not be a reduction in their family allowance cheque.

He gave out empty Kraft Dinner boxes to people who were there, in particular a poor mother with her child. He appeared at the behest of a low income support group from Ottawa. He was here to show the feeling which low income people have that this was not really Father Christmas but the Grinch in disguise-a green monster. I would not hesitate to say that this was a green monster who represents the Hon. Member who comes from the hills of Provencher who wants to steal Christmas from children, mothers and, of course, families. The message which is being given out by the Conservative Government is that it will cut the value of the family allowance for Canada's children and families and, in particular, mothers who are struggling so hard to raise children. The Government is doing this as a Christmas present.
While this was going on Members of Parliament, at least those of us who sit in Opposition, continued to present petitions, something which we have been doing now for weeks. We have presented hundreds of petitions with tens of thousands of signatures on them which have been sent to us from people all across Canada. They continue to flood into Members' offices, at least into mine, every day. We had hoped that, as a result of this particular protest and appeal from Canadians, the Minister, like the Grinch, would perhaps have his heart warmed and reconsider, or at least delay until after Christmas, taking any action with respect to Bill C-70. Of course, this morning we know what the answer is.
As a Christmas present to Canada's children, the Government has brought in time allocation which will force us to push through this Bill. This is only a repeat of what the Government has done since the introduction of Bill C-70. It brought in time allocation when we first debated the Bill at second reading stage. It imposed time allocation when there was no need for it. Then, when the Bill was before the committee, the Government reduced the number of weeks which had been allowed for witnesses to appear before the committee. It refused to hear from certain witnesses who had appealed to appear before it. I am thinking particularly of groups which are very concerned about the missing children section of the Bill and the child find groups which wanted to appear. I have before me petitions from about seven or eight of those groups from across Canada who appealed to the Minister to let them be heard. Of course, the committee refused to hear them on the advice of the Minister. Again, we had time allocation in that respect.
Native women were not heard. Native groups which suffer the greatest poverty in the country and which also have much larger families depend on a fully indexed family allowance for their families. They were not heard from. The Government brought in time allocation with respect to the proceedings of the committee and here we see it being imposed again at the report stage of the Bill. I think this is an absolute disgrace. It shows the insincerity and the mess which the Government is perpetuating.
The Minister has said over and over again that his social policy was to reinforce families. He has said that he cares about families and that he supports them. Yet, as a result of this Bill, he is attacking them. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), the Minister responsible for the status of women and, in fact, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have said that women will be an important priority of the Government. Yet they were responsible for presenting a Bill the first thing this fall that attacks women. It attacks particularly low income women and those women are stuggling to raise children on their own.
The Minister can laugh, but it is no laughing matter to mothers across Canada who will see a reduction in their family allowance benefits as a result of this measure.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to listen to the New Democratic Party talk about how terrible things are in Canada today, because consumer spending has never hit such heights. I suggest that those Hon. Members wander over to some of the shopping centres and take a look at the stores which are just jammed with people. That does not indicate that this country is going to rack and ruin.
There is certainly no hypocrite like a Grit hypocrite. I just want to set the record straight. The family allowance will now be increased by the annual increase in the consumer price index in excess of 3 per cent. That is up, not down. The principle of universality is maintained. And we are going to maintain universality. It is interesting to read what a top Grit has been saying. "Abandon universality, Liberals told", by a former Liberal cabinet Minister, Otto Lang. He wants universality abolished. It is interesting to note the double standards of the Liberals. Their hidden agenda probably includes the abolishment of universality.
The child tax credit, which is of particular benefit to low income families, will be increased by 36 per cent, from $384 in 1985 to $524 in 1988. In 1986 there will be a $70 increase, raising the credit from $384 to $454 per child. In 1987, there will be a further $35 increase. In 1988 there will be an additional $35 increase. The child tax exemption, which is of particular benefit to high income families, will be reduced, so we are not looking after the rich as someone mentioned here a moment ago. It will be reduced by almost half from $710 to about $380, to equal the amount of family allowances. These changes will enhance the support provided to low income families while reducing benefits to higher income families, thus correcting inequities in the existing system.
Speaking of taxes, my Province of Manitoba, which has a New Democratic Government, has the highest taxes in Canada. That is really tough on the poor. The NDP policy is "tax, tax, tax". Manitoba has the highest taxes in the country. Its payroll taxes put a burden on employers so they cannot employ more people. That is how the NDP governs in Manitoba. It makes it really difficult for everyone.
This Government is committed to protect and improve social programs in Canada. We are now spending more on the social envelope than on any other envelope. The total social spending will rise by $4 billion, to $46.7 billion, close to half of total government expenditures. In this vein, the Government has expanded the eligibility for the spouses' allowance, benefiting 85,000 younger widows and widowers who had previously not qualified for benefits. So more people are going to benefit, not less.
Veterans' benefits have been improved for more than 140,000 Canadians and tax assistance has been extended to 185,000 disabled Canadians. So there is no cut-back in social programs in this country.

1 would like now to comment on the Grit hypocrisy. Between 1974-75 and 1984-85, the Grits reduced spending on social programs. They were not worried about the aged or the poor at that time. Spending on social programs dropped from 50 per cent of federal expenditures to 43 per cent. So that tells us they are against the poor.
Prior to 1973 the Liberal Government did not index family allowances at all. That is real hypocrisy. In 1976, the Grits suspended the indexation of family allowances for a full year. With respect to the petitions they have been distributing, I wonder if they have provided those people with this kind of information. I will bet not.
On January 1, 1979, the Grits reduced family allowances by 20 per cent. How come they are not telling the people that? They should put that on the petitions they are spreading around-those phonies. In 1983-84, the Grits brought in their six and five program, which dramatically reduced inflation protection at a time of rampant inflation. They should put that at the top of their petitions.
To give a clear indication that the poor are not being neglected and social spending is certainly not dropping in this country, I will read a list of the social programs we have in this country: Canada Assistance Plan, provincial tax credits, veterans' allowance, social assistance to on-reserve Indians, guaranteed income supplement and spouses' allowance, child tax credit, social housing, child care expense deduction, family allowance, child tax exemption, assistance to the married and equivalent to married, unemployment insurance, training allowance, workers' compensation, employment expense deduction, and seven different programs for the elderly. This comes to a total in federal and provincial spending of $61.6 billion. We are doing this despite the problem we have inherited from the Grits, the huge debt load for which the Leader of the Grits is responsible, that architect of the uncontrolled spending in this country. We are spending $61.6 billion, Mr. Speaker, and our problem is to try to maintain that amount, but I have no doubt we will certainly maintain it.
There is no shortage of spending on social programs in this country. The $61.6 billion does not include what municipalities are spending on social assistance. The Grits talk about how upset the seniors were when we were going to reduce indexing somewhat. What the seniors said to me was: "At least you listen". In the past, when the Grits were reducing pensions, they certainly did not listen. When I explained to these people the debt problem, and I gave them the entire explanation and all the information, then they realized how serious a problem it is. They want to co-operate. This is the kind of information Members opposite should be putting on their petitions. Explain everything to these people. Show them the amount being spent. Give them all the information.

At the heart of this issue, the reason why the parliamentary Opposition are so fundamentally and adamantly opposed to the measures put forward in Bill C-70, is the fact that these measures do not address the major issue we began discussing at the time we started the debate on universality, the issue of fairness. This Government began the debate based on the concept of putting in place more equity and fairness in the package of child benefits. However, it then comes forward with Bill C-70 which will, along with the tax measures in Bill C-84, impact severely on the low and middle-income earners of this country. That is an affront to the intelligence of all Members of this House, including the Government back-benchers. I note that those back-benchers have been conspicuously silent in this debate from the very beginning through to May 23.
I do not want to but I am going to ask that Members recall some of the words they used when they were in opposition four and five years ago and there was some discussion about the possibility of deindexing the tax system. Deindexing, they said, is a scheme to guarantee that everyone will pay higher federal income taxes year after year after year. The numbers I have chosen here are numbers which have been used in the debate previously and they are undisputed. The net effect of plans to deindex family allowances and personal income taxes and fully implement the budget proposals means the following. If you have a family income of $15,000 a year you are going to pay an additional $1,879 in taxes over the next five years as a result of those two Bills alone. A family earning $35,000, which StatsCan indicates is a middle-income family, will pay an additional $3,452 in taxes. However, what happens to the family who earns $80,000 a year? They will only pay an additional $1,125 in taxes. In other words, the low and middle-income earners will pay more in taxes than the family with an $80,000 a year income. That is why the Opposition in this Parliament stand adamantly opposed not only to deindexation of family allowances but also to many of the measures in the May 23 Budget concerning taxes.
How in heaven's name can we justify a social policy which will widen the gap between the rich and the poor? It is evident that that is the Conservative social policy and it reflects the lack of a common sense approach to the difficulties faced by this country. We on this side of the House in the Opposition recognize that the deficit is a problem which has to be addressed by whichever Party is in power. However, if you are attempting to create the political will in this country to undertake the necessary reforms, you certainly do not do it with a Budget which widens the gap between the rich and the poor in our society.
I will respect the rules of the House and not wave an ad that I saw in The Citizen in Ottawa several days ago. I think most Members in the House have seen it. It is a full page ad which shows a well-to-do middle-aged couple. The wife is wearing a mink and the husband is wearing a tuxedo. The caption reads: "Buy your wife a condo for Christmas". The ad goes on to explain the various tax breaks that the Budget of May 23 will give to that group. The disparity in the country between the poor and the rich is the major reason we are fundamentally opposed to the social policy direction which the Conservative Government has undertaken since it assumed office in September of 1984.
To be a competent Opposition we should be able to put forward amendments to the Bill which we feel would improve the legislation. The recommendation that we made last spring to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs were totally ignored by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) when he finally brought forward his plan to deindex the family allowance. More important, when Bill C-70, which we are debating on the floor of the House today, was referred to the committee, members of the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party put forward a series of amendments to it which we knew would significantly improve the Bill. Yet, the Conservative majority on that committee steadfastly refused every amendment we put forward. They did not allow certain groups which both opposition Parties recommended be allowed to testify to do so.

Why is it the Government, which supposedly placed such a high value on consultation, has now introduced time allocation on this Bill to deindex the family allowance? Why did the Government, which put so much value on consultation, refuse to listen to every major social agency in the country that represents the poor and middle income people and have said that the plan to deindex the family allowance and, in particular, the technicalities of the way in which the Government is going to do so, is going to result in a new child benefit package that will help no one after 1989? The Government misleads the public when it indicates that next month's cheque will be larger than this month's cheque. It is true that it will be larger by 31 cents. That includes families earning $9,000 a year and those earning $15,000 a year. That is at the heart of the matter, Mr. Speaker.
The Government does not seem to place any importance on the fact that its policies will widen the gap between the rich and the poor in our society. I predict that, unless the Government reverses this trend, there will be a disturbing trend of increasing violence in our society which tolerates the rich getting richer and the poor getting poorer on the backs of the middle-income.

Indeed, 1 think the person who wrote that poem really put his finger on the matter. We have seen in the last number of weeks, and are seeing again today, a very blatant display of the real priorities of the Government.
Members of the Government have justified moving closure on this motion because there are other pieces of legislation with which the House must deal. What are those other pieces of important legislation to which they refer? One of those important pieces of legislation which they say must be passed is the Bill to bail out the banks and provide some $800 million to bail out uninsured depositors, many of whom are foreign bankers and large banking concerns in this country.
Another piece of legislation which they say must be passed is a Bill to give half a million dollars in tax free capital gains to the wheelers and dealers in this country.
It is blatantly obvious that the priority of the Government is to spend some $800 million to bail out large sophisticated depositors who had money on deposit at the Canadian Commercial Bank because they could get a half point higher interest at that bank. It is to provide a half million dollars tax free to people who speculate in condominiums, jewellery and other luxuries. That is the priority of the Government. Today we are seeing a blatant transfer of weatlh from the poor and middle class of this country to the well-to-do and filthy rich of this country. It is shameful. The Minister and Government Members laugh as they sit in their comfortable seats. Let me warn them that it will be the mothers of this country who will have the last laugh come the next election. They will not forget the blatant transfer of wealth which the Government has perpetuated with the Budget and the tax measures that it has introduced. Of course, this is all being done in the name of fighting the deficit. There is no doubt the deficit is a serious problem, Mr. Speaker. But to justify nickel and diming mothers and families in the name of fighting the deficit is a disgraceful farce. It will not be believed by the people. People will not believe that nickel and diming mothers and children will effectively put a dent in the deficit when the Government is forking over billions of dollars to the banks.
The Government is allowing capital gains. What about the $32 billion or $33 billion in deferred taxes alone that the large corporations owe to the Government? Corporations have been able to defer taxes from year to year until now and most of the large amounts now owing to the Government are being written off.
Canadians will not be hoodwinked. They know what is going on. If the Government were genuinely sincere in reducing the deficit, the Government would go to the people who have the ability to pay and who legally owe the money and would start collecting from them. Instead the poor are getting nicked.
The other argument the Government uses is that a universal scheme-the family allowance-has a lot of money going to the well to do. A study recently released by the Canadian Council on Social Development explodes this myth. It pointed out that families earning the average income or less-and the average income for a family estimated in 1984 is some $35,000-will be losing the bulk of the money that would have normally gone to them through the family allowance.
When you look at the figures you begin to realize that those whose incomes are $50,000 or more only account for 12 per cent of what the Government will save on this measure. The people who earn less than $50,000 a year will lose some 78 per cent of what the Government will save in this measure. They are the ones who will pay.
It is obscene for a Government to elect to save money through programs like the deindexing of family allowance while it introduces regressive tax measures, such as the capital gains measure. It is obscene for any civilized country so blatantly to take from the poor and give to the rich. It goes against our tradition and our sense of values. It is, as 1 mentioned before, an obscenity. Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that the Government which started out with such popular support is now seeing its popularity decrease month after month after month?
We have seen and heard groups that have gone public as opposing this tax measure. We have received petitions signed by hundreds of thousands of people. The Family Service Bureau has publicly come out against the measure. So have the National Action Committee, the Vanier Institute of the Family, the Canadian Council on Children and Youth, the Canadian Council on Social Development and the churches. The Government is prepared to ignore this wide representation of Canadians and instead is listening to the pleas of the well-to-do.
Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, and let me remind the Government, that the time will come to face the public, and the public will not forget.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-70
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as 1 listened to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) defend this indefensible proposal by the so-called Progressive Conservative Government, I wondered if he would have made the same speech in an earlier Parliament when he represented the constituency of Winnipeg-St. James. In that constituency, unlike the constituency which he now represents that includes in its boundaries the wealthiest people in Metropolitan Winnipeg, he represented some poor people. 1 wonder whether he would have made the same speech then. I wonder whether he would make the same speech if he took the time when in Winnipeg to visit some of the church agencies which are handing out food baskets to people who are hungry, or some of the centres which provide meals for people who are hungry, or some of the schools in the core area of Winnipeg which have nutrition programs so that some of the children attending those schools get their only decent meal of the day. That is the situation in Winnipeg.
It is because of those kinds of situations, because we know how many people are in need and how many children are in need that we are so unalterably opposed to what the Government wants to do, insists on doing and brings in closure to achieve its aim.
From the end of World War II to about 1975, Canadian people and the political Parties which represented them federally and provincially seemed to agree that the country was wealthy enough and had the ability to provide a whole series of programs to meet basic needs and to put in place a floor below which people would not have to live. Therefore, we established the Unemployment Insurance Program and improved the Old Age Security Program. We established the Canada Pension Plan and provided universal hospital and medical insurance. We brought in the Canada Assistance Program under which the federal Government shared with the provincial Governments the cost of providing for basic needs of people who are unemployed or unable to work because of illness.
The Family Allowance Program was a fundamental part of the whole range of programs which we provided to the Canadian people. Until about 1975, there seemed to be a consensus
that these programs should not only be continued but should be improved upon and expanded. Beginning in 1975 when the Canadian economy, like the economy of the rest of the world, began to experience serious problems, we began to see the beginnings of cut-backs. We saw a new and more onerous provisions imposed on the Unemployment Insurance Program. Doctors began to extra bill when provinces did not provide in their medical insurance plans enough money to pay doctors what they thought they should get. The Liberal Government put the six and five cap on programs including the Family Allowance Program.
During the last federal election campaign, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that social programs were a sacred trust. He said that if the Conservative Party formed a Government, it would not only maintain the programs but would improve upon them. What we have seen since the election of the Conservative Government has been the exact reverse.
We have seen, in the Conservative Government's supposed determination to reduce the deficit which it claims is higher than the country can afford, that the Government is determined to impose cuts on a whole series of programs. We know about the new restrictions and cuts in unemployment insurance benefits. We know that the Government proposed to deindex old age pensions. Fortunately for the senior citizens, we were able to mount the kind of campaign that made the Government realize that there would be tremendous adverse political consequences if it proceeded with that proposal, so the Government backed down. However, as we can see today by this closure motion, the Government is determined to deindex family allowances.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie), in his speech, tried to confuse the issue again by saying that family allowance benefits would increase. Of course they will increase. If the cost of living increases next year, as it seems to have increased this year, by 4 per cent, the family allowance benefits will increase by 1 per cent rather than 4 per cent. The amount Canadians will receive will decrease by 3 per cent in real value. If the cost of living goes up by 4 per cent in each year, and that is a relatively modest estimate as in the past it has risen by 10, 12 and 14 per cent, it is pretty obvious that the real value of the family allowance benefits will decrease throughout the years.
Why has the Government proposed to do this? It is because the Government says that we must reduce the deficit. What the Government is doing has been criticised by every single agency and group which is interested in the welfare of children and families. Let me put on the record a couple of the views of organizations which know a great deal more about the needs of families and children than the Conservative Government and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) who brought forward this proposal. The Canadian Council on Children and Youth put out a press release dated December 12, 1985, which indicated the following:
"By de-indexing family allowances, reducing the child tax credit and lowering the income level at which families are taxed on the child tax credit, the
December 19, 1985

Government of Canada is stating that Canadian parents are getting too much to raise their children."
"Nothing could be farther from the truth," said Brian Ward, executive director of the Canadian Council on Children and Youth. There are 6.3 million in Canada, and a shocking 20 per cent of them or 1.2 million are living in poor families.
I would invite the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine to join me in visiting some of these families to see what the proposal he is supporting will mean to them.
Again on December 12, 1985, the Vanier Institute of the Family said the following:
"Under their Christmas trees this year, parents will find a present to them from the federal government, a present wrapped in the prosaic prose of Bill C-70 which proposes to partially deindex Family Allowances."
The Institute goes on to say:
"It proposes a change that, over time, will make the Family Allowance program worth very little to Canadian families."
If the people of Canada have to tighten their belts, any Canadian Government which really cared about the people of Canada would see that the belt tightening would be equitable and would be done by those who could afford it most. What do we see? We know that there are something like 8,000 Canadians who had taxable incomes of over $50,000 and 270 Canadians who had taxable incomes of over $200,000 who did not pay a penny in income tax for the last year for which figures are available.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has announced that he is bringing in a minimum tax, a proposal which we urged for years and which the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) endorsed during the federal election campaign. We welcome that announcement but now that we have had an opportunity to look at some of the fine print, we realize that what the Minister is proposing is a great deal less than it seems to be.
It is not only individual Canadians who have not been required to do their fair share of belt tightening. Dome Petroleum Limited, under terms of a special law that gives the Cabinet almost unlimited powers to skirt the Income Tax Act, was given a tax break that could save the company up to $1 billion by 1990 on taxes payable by its subsidiary, Hudson's Bay Oil & Gas. If I am not mistaken, that was done under the former Liberal Government, so there is not much difference between the Liberals and the Conservatives.
Petro-Canada saved $250 million in taxes on its 1981 takeover of Petro-Fina Limited after the Liberal Government pushed through retroactive legislation in January 1984 to iron out a wrinkle that would have denied Petro-Canada tax breaks. According to the Auditor General, this extra $250 million is in addition to another bit of paperwork under which Petro-Fina's Belgian shareholders avoided about $200 million in taxes. As well, Olympia & York Corporation, when it purchased Gulf Canada, was able to use the loopholes in the tax system to reduce its taxes by between $500 million and $600 million.
The few illustrations given simply prove that the Government, while it talks about the need to reduce the deficit and
Time Allocation
the need to realize that we will not be able to have the same kind of benefits that were implemented over the many years, and while it talks about the need for ordinary people to tighten their belts, is continuing the same kind of policies which the former Liberal Government implemented and which this Government has expanded upon. An example of this is the $500,000 capital gains tax provision. The percentage of Canadians who can benefit from that provision is very small. It has been estimated that only 7 per cent of Canadians can benefit from this Government proposal which will cost the people of Canada hundreds of millions of dollars. It is only for the wealthy, while this reduction in family allowance benefits is only for ordinary Canadians.
Again, we see the Government, as we so frequently saw Liberal Governments, asking ordinary Canadians to make sacrifices and to pay a much higher percentage of their taxes to meet the requirements of the Government. At the same time the people in higher income tax brackets and large corporations are permitted to avoid, to a large extent, their fair share of what is required.
Again I say, as members of my Party have said, that the first time the Government brought forward this proposal we opposed it. We intend to continue to oppose it. We intend to alert the Canadian people to what is happening. We intend to remind them now and in the years to come until the next election who is responsible for the retrograde provisions which are included in this proposal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, here we go again-another time allocation order. Closure has been imposed once more. More and more it is becoming the pattern, a matter of course, for this Government with its massive majority which surrounds the Opposition on all sides. More and more we are seeing time allocation orders with respect to debate on important principles.
I have said before, and I repeat, that under all circumstances time allocation is not objectionable. There are certain circumstances in which it can be quite legitimately justified. For example, let us suppose that there was a program or policy which was central to the philosophy of a political Party which was elected to power. In this instance, after due debate, let us suppose it was decided to bring in time allocation with respect to this central policy. I think Members of the House can understand and accept that. I have already used the illustration of Investment Canada replacing the Foreign Investment Review Agency. During the election campaign members of the Conservative Party made it clear that they did not believe in having a monitoring agency look at foreign takeovers in the country. They wanted to open the doors wide and let foreign investors come in and buy whatever they wanted to buy. They brought in a Bill to deal with this philosophy early in their mandate and they imposed time allocation on it. I disagreed with the Bill and argued against it. However, I can understand why the Government would use time allocation with respect to su8h a provision.

December 19, 1985
Time Allocation
I now wish to turn to the matter of time allocation. Is it true that the central policy of the Conservative Government is to begin the dismantling of the Canadian social security system? Is that the central policy of the Conservative Party now that it is in government? It certainly appears to me that it is. Yet, I remember well that catchy phrase used by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was asked repeatedly across the country about our social security system. He was asked: "Sir, is it under any threat by you?" He replied with that very memorable phrase: "No. This is a sacred trust". That question was asked for good reason since there has always been a suspicion in the country that the Conservative Party does not really believe in a comprehensive social security system. That is a suspicion which lingers in the minds of Canadians. That is why they wanted to be assured before they voted in the last federal election that our system would not be dismantled. They were given that assurance and we are now beginning to dismantle it. In order to get on with the dismantling, time allocation has been imposed.
I would like to ask the question: When is there sufficient debate on a Bill which is as controversial as this one? I suppose there are many answers to my question. I believe debate should not come to an end until the public has been made fully aware of the implications of a piece of legislation. That takes some time. After all, Canadians do not focus all of their attention all of the time on the House of Commons. They have jobs to do. They have families to raise. They have recreational pursuits to follow. They just do not spend all their time following the proceedings of the House. That is why they have sent us here. They say: "Look. We do not have time. We have important things to do. Go down there and keep an eye on those fellows. See what they are doing. Watch over them for us". Even though technology has given us an effective communications system, it still takes time to inform the public fully with respect to what is being done as a result of legislation which is introduced in the House. I would say that although the public is catching up quickly to what Bill C-70 means, it still needs additional time. That is what the Opposition is providing-additional time to inform the public and make it completely aware of what is involved in Bill C-70.
I argue that the Government has failed to make its case with respect to the validity of Bill C-70. We know that because petitions continue to pour in. They have not all been read, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) argues that the House of Commons is having its time wasted because petitions are being read. He fails to understand what Parliament is all about. Do not the people of Canada who have become aware that a certain piece of legislation is threatening them have the right to petition the House of Commons? Do they not have the right to have their petitions read here in this place? They certainly do. It is a fundamental right. It is a basic right. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine who suggests otherwise really reveals that even after all his time here he has failed to grasp the importance of the parliamentary system.
I wish to say that the petitions which have been presented have not only been presented by members of the Opposition. Some petitions have been presented by those who sit on the benches in the bookends. Those Government Members have had the courage to say that their constituents have a right to petition the House of Commons with respect to Bill C-70.
The Minister has said: "The Opposition is getting it all wrong. The family allowance will be increased". As my colleague just mentioned a few moments ago, the family allowance will be increased by 31 cents. At the same time we know that the rate of inflation has increased by 4 per cent. Therefore, the buying power of the family allowance cheque which will be sent to families in January will be much less. The Government knows that. It is a kind of callous misinformation for the Minister to suggest that the family allowance will be increased.
When the legislative committee met and representatives of the Canadian Labour Congress appeared before it, they pointed out clearly that the social security system and, in particular, the family allowance, will deteriorate and be undermined over a period of time. They gave this fact. They said that over a 20-year period, if one assumes a rate of inflation of only 3 per cent, and if we use 1985 dollars, today's $32 family allowance cheque will be worth only $18 in terms of its spending power in 20 years' time. This is a standard way of proceeding for the purpose of making such a projection. The child tax credit about which the Minister likes to argue will offset this decrease. He has said: "Don't forget the child tax credit". The Canadian Labour Congress looked at that as well and stated that in that same period of time, the Child Tax Credit will go from $384 in spending power to $326. The family income level for those who can qualify for this universal benefit will go from $26,500 today down to $13,800.
This Government has been rather clever in that the present formula for the child tax credit will improve for a three-year period. That cannot be denied. From 1987 to 1990, there will be an improvement in the child tax credit. But what the Government has not been forthright about is what happens after 1990. What happens to the child tax credit in 1991? We have looked at this area very carefully and we know that in 1991, deindexation will cause poor families to fall further and further behind in their buying power. We know that after that time the child tax credit, instead of increasing, will start to go down.
The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women has called these changes unfair and unjust. It goes on to point out that the present system-the system this Government is changing-of family allowances fully indexed to the cost of living and taxed back from the wealthy by a progressive tax system, is clearly effective in transferring income from wealthy families to poorer ones. That is exactly what is the essential and primary role of any Government. What the Government does in allowing the family allowance cheque to deteriorate is to weaken one of the most prominent universal social programs
December 19, 1985

in the country. I call upon the Government and the Minister to let the present system of universal fully indexed family allowances be maintained. 1 ask that the increase in the child tax credit be not only for a short duration of three years but that it continue to increase to meet the genuine needs of families and their children in the future. I ask that the total amount of money spent to benefit families and children not be reduced but in fact increased.
1 know why members of the Government would not want to listen to Liberals or New Democrats. I heard the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) spit out the word "Grit" with all the anger he could muster. 1 could understand that, but I wonder if that Hon. cial Governments on this question. It is a very serious constitutional question. Does the Government have the authority to do that in the first place? maintopic: OPPOSITION TO USE OF DEPO-PROVERA AS CONTRACEPTIVE
OPPOSITION TO USE OF DEPO-PROVERA AS CONTRACEPTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Depo-Provera is a hormone drug which can be used as an injectable contraceptive. Among its reported side effects are blood clots, high blood pressure, irregular bleeding, excessive weight gain, severe depression, and hair loss. The long-term effects are not known at this time, but animal and clinical tests indicate infertility and increased risk of cancer and heart disease.
The U.S. Federal Drug Administration refused to approve Depo-Provera as a contraceptive in 1974, 1978, and again in 1983. Some 62 groups in Canada have formed a coalition to demand public hearings into this issue which is too important to be decided behind closed doors where the Minister's officials listen only to the company's story. I call upon the Minister to release the documents and research on which the advisory committee made its recommendation, and to open up the entire process to the public.
It has also come to my attention that this drug is being used on mentally retarded teenagers and other young people considered to be juvenile delinquents. This is not only unacceptable by any standard, it is immoral. I call upon the Minister to ban the use of this drug in Canada immediately and specifically prohibit its use on young children who are developmentally handicapped or are juvenile delinquents, until it has been proven safe.

subtopic: TIMMINS, ONT.-ACQUISITION OF KIDD CREEK MINES BY FALCONBRIDGELTD.
TIMMINS, ONT.-ACQUISITION OF KIDD CREEK MINES BY FALCONBRIDGELTD.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to speak today about the recent acquisition of Kidd Creek Mines Ltd. by Falconbridge Ltd. The main asset of the company is an ore body in Timmins, the major community in my riding. Kidd Creek is the major employer in Timmins. Workers, suppliers and others have called my office and I want to assure them and the community that we feel the transaction will be a positive one. We have spoken to various people about this matter and all feel the local mining industry will be strengthened and Falconbridge will broaden its economic base.
We have been told that in the past Falconbridge has had a hands-off policy toward its wholly-owned subsidiaries, and we expect that to continue. Therefore the community can look forward to dealing with the same excellent management team at Kidd Creek which has operated the mine for the past few years. This team will now be seconded by the management team at Falconbridge, headed by President Bill James, who is also President of the Mining Association of Canada.
We would draw to the community's attention that the other major shareholder in Falconbridge is Dome Mines Ltd. As a result, people are available to Falconbridge who are very familiar with Timmins and local conditions. We have the same rich ore body, the same management team, enriched by those from Falconbridge and Dome, and the same highly trained and dedicated workforce, along with one of the most modern smelters in the world. Therefore the Kidd Creek operation and Timmins can look forward to the future with confidence.
December 19, 1985

subtopic: BENEFIT OF CAPITAL GAINS TAX EXEMPTION TO OLDER FARMERS
BENEFIT OF CAPITAL GAINS TAX EXEMPTION TO OLDER FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the May Budget provided that a farmer, to qualify for the immediate $500,000 capital gains exemption, had to have farmed the land for at least five years since 1972. Older Canadians who farmed for many years, but not for five years since 1972, expressed concern. I congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) for listening to these concerns and acting by eliminating the reference to 1972, thereby expanding the definition of farm property qualifying for the immediate $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption.
Now, effective January 1, 1985, land owned by the taxpayer and used by him, his spouse or children in the business of farming in Canada, either in the year of sale or in at least five years during which the property was owned by the taxpayer or his family, will qualify. Older Canadians who may have rented out their land in recent years, but who have farmed for at least five years, will now enjoy the immediate exemption retroactive to January 1, 1985.
Livestock drought assistance, fuel tax rebates, crop insurance, western grain stabilization, crop disaster assistance, the domestic wheat reference, the Soviet grain agreement, and the capital gains exemption, are but a few of the many responsible agricultural initiatives put forward by the Government-a Government that listens and acts.

subtopic: CLIMATIC CHANGES-CONSEQUENCES OF PROJECTED GREENHOUSE EFFECT
CLIMATIC CHANGES-CONSEQUENCES OF PROJECTED GREENHOUSE EFFECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this House and the present Government will be well advised to start plans and policies that will take into account the consequences of the greenhouse effect which, according to scientists, will cause temperatures to rise by two or three degrees centigrade around the globe over the next 70 years. Many will be the consequences of the warming-up trend. For instance, agriculture will shift northward. In southern Canada lands presently used for agriculture could be lost because of dryness. Therefore water will become more and more precious because our needs will increase considerably.
As a consequence of these climatic changes we will have to learn to manage our water better, to squander less and, most of all, not to yield to pressures for export and diversions of fresh water. Water conservation is a practice we should adopt. We should also drastically improve ways of controlling and regulating what we discharge into water so as to protect water quality.
At present, Mr. Speaker, water is perceived to be an abundant commodity. As our climate warms up, water will gradually become a commodity in short supply. This trend need not be a disaster provided we plan and manage well the transition to a warmer climate by a judicious use of our water resources and by becoming a water-efficient society.

Mr. Speaker, on December 13 the United Nations General Assembly passed its first resolution expressing deep concern over "specific and detailed allegations of human rights violations in Iran". The resolution, 1 am proud to say, was initiated by Canada and the Netherlands, with 10 other countries co-sponsoring it. The resolution comments on the summary executions, torture, and oppression of religious minorities in Iran, and endorses continued monitoring of the situation.
Iran has been asked to extend full co-operation which, up until now, it has refused, including not allowing the U.N. Special Representative on Human Rights to visit Iran. We are told that it is of tremendous help to the Bahai's and other oppressed minorities in Iran to know that they have not been forgotten by the world, even when they are apparently without rights in their own country.
I urge the House of Commons and the Government of Canada to remain fully informed on this grievous situation and to support the Canadian delegation at the U.N. in maintaining the vigilant and courageous international leadership by which it has been distinguishing itself on this issue in its efforts to end persecution and atrocities in Iran.

subtopic: PRESERVATION OF SAFETY STANDARDS IN DEREGULATION PROCESS
PRESERVATION OF SAFETY STANDARDS IN DEREGULATION PROCESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians mourn the recent tragedy of the crash of the DC-8 at Gander, Newfoundland. At the moment the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board and the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration are working together to determine the cause of this disaster. To date, the cause has not been found.
In wake of such a tragedy the Opposition have insinuated that with the Government's current proposals for economic regulatory reform of Canada's transportation sector, many more aviation accidents will occur. I find such insinuations morally reprehensible.
The Government will make a lot of changes to our regulatory framework but it will never allow safety standards for transportation services to be sacrificed for economic expediency. For the past several weeks the parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport has listened to the recommendations and concerns of many interested parties. During its entire lengthy proceedings, the committee stressed to all parties that safety standards would not be debated.
Canada's high level of safety standards is being maintained and has been enhanced. An example of this is the Government's passage of Bill C-36, an Act to amend the Aeronautics Act. As the Minister of Transport stated in the preface of his policy paper entitled Freedom to Move: "I would like to indicate unequivocally that the Government will neither propose nor permit any economic regulatory reform that might be detrimental to safety standards".
I hope that certain members of the Opposition who have an inclination for distorting the truth will take heed of the Minister's words and not try to induce panic into the Canadian public regarding transportation safety standards.

EFFECT OF CHANGE ON MINERS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 bring to the attention of the House an unfair situation involving my constituents in the Hemlo Gold find area of northern Ontario. It is an unfairness created as a consequence of the May 23 Budget.
The employees of the Teck-Corona Mine, near Marathon, as a result of the May 23 Budget have been divided into two groups: one group of 51 employees are forced to pay tax on a benefit derived from the company, a benefit in the form of a housing loan; at the same time another group of 49 employees with the same company will be receiving a non-taxable benefit from the same type of loan. This is all because of an income tax change which was included in the last federal Budget.
The company has been hiring its staff over the past year and a half. Therefore, many employees bought their houses before May 23. When Teck-Corona suggested that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) allow all housing loans to be exempt as of May 23, the Minister stated in a letter that an extension of this kind would represent an additional tax expenditure and would add significantly to the deficit. I doubt the validity of that assertion.
More important, we have a new tax measure which creates inequity among employees working for the same company and living in the very same community.
Therefore I ask that the Minister of Finance immediately reconsider his initial response. Let there be a grandfather clause in this tax relief measure.

December 19, 1985

and teenagers are a cash-poor group who need unlimited local calling to maintain healthy social Ivies. And, of course, I need not tell any Member in this place about the devastating effect local calling charges would have on small business throughout Canada.

speechtext:
-I would like to make a preliminary report on the situation in the St. Clair River based on the most up-to-date information as of 3.10 this afternoon. It should reassure both the Canadian public and Members of the House that the federal Department of the Environment is moving, in co-operation with the Opposition and the Government of Ontario, on all fronts to remove and identify the source of the tarry substance that is disfiguring the river and causing concern about the quality of the drinking water of thousands of Canadians.
I should explain that this statement is an interim one only, because the situation has proved to be more complex than the investigative team originally thought. Moreover, ongoing clean-up of the river has been complicated by bad weather. Since the House will not be meeting until after the New Year, as of tomorrow, I thought that nevertheless it would be useful to report on the findings to date.
To put the matter into context, let me briefly review the sequence of events in the St. Clair River. Certain tarry substances have been noted in the river since the mid-1970s. Continuous sampling has taken place, but it was not until two years ago that more sophisticated analytical methods were developed for this type of natural phenomenon. In 1984, the Great Lakes Institute, acting on behalf of both the federal Department of the Environment and the Ontario Ministry of the Environment, conducted a survey to identify "hot spots" in the St. Clair River. In August, 1984, a sample of the tarry substance was submitted to the Ontario Ministry of the Environment for analysis. In mid-August of this year, the tests were completed and, based on the results, additional sampling was authorized.
Between August 13 and August 16 of this Year, Dow Chemical situated on the river, spilled perchloroethylene, of which all but 2,500 gallons was recaptured. My first act, after
my appointment as Minister of the Environment on August 19, was to instruct department officials to offer full scientific and technical advice to their Ontario colleagues in order to clean up the remainder of the spill.
By November 1, information from officials of the Department of the Environment made it clear to me that the problem was much more complex and potentially more serious than just the spill itself. That same day I set up a team of scientists whose only task since then has been to identify all the components of the so-called blob and to identify other pollution problems in the St. Clair River, locate their origins and begin working on solutions to them. That analytical team, I might say, includes Canada's most distinguished scientists in every relevant field-organic chemistry, hydro-dynamics, hydrogeology, pollution enginering, diving and underwater photography to mention just a few. There are more than 50 scientists in all working literally seven days a week on the St. Clair River problem. Moreover, because our American neighbours have a direct stake in the purity of the St. Clair River, I have kept Lee Thomas, Director of the Environmental Protection Agency in the United States, fully informed, and his scientists are giving my Department their complete co-operation.
In that first week of November, the CSS Advent, Environment Canada's scientific research vessel, was dispatched to the St. Clair River. Underwater photography gave us the first clear picture of the extent of the pollution there. Divers immediately began collecting samples from the riverbed and these have now been analysed in the laboratories of the National Water Research Institute. The scientific team has completed more than 2,000 analyses for a full range of organic pollutants.
On the basis of those analyses, the scientific team, established on November 1, is now integrating and interpreting data in order to provide a complete and coherent picture of the St. Clair River. By January 20, I expect to have their report and be able to release it to the House, and through the House, to the Canadian public.
On the basis of the work done to date, we do know that the so-called blob comprises extremely high concentrations of perchloroethylene and carbon tetrachloride. The two chemicals are used as dry-cleaning solvents and, in fact, it is the very properties that render them useful in dry-cleaning that make them obnoxious in drinking water. In this case, they have absorbed other contaminants throughout the St. Clair River into themselves and of course compounded the magnitude of the tarry-like substance that is now being vacuumed.
Let me turn now to private sector involvement in the St. Clair problem and the context in which it exists.
First, every Member of the House, and in fact every person in the country, has to recognize that we live in a chemical society. Today there are more than 60,000 chemicals being used in the world's trade and commerce, and more than 1,000 new compounds are being introduced annually. Each year, companies in North America produce more than a ton of chemicals for each man, woman and child living on the entire continent.
December 19, 1985

In Canada, economic and historical forces have combined to create a chemical valley along the St. Clair River and it includes Dow Chemical Canada Limited. We know that a key to the current problem is a spill of perchloroethylene by Dow between August 13 and August 16, 1985. Moreover, for many years, Dow disposed of chemical waste by placing them in abandoned salt caverns that lie below the riverbed. Other companies injected their wastes into the shallower Detroit Formation. 1 should stress that the companies' waste disposal methods were consistent with what was understood at the time to be safe.
Dow has been vacuuming the St. Clair River since concern first focused on the tarry material and is continuing to do so to this day. An area approximately 30 metres square is being cleaned. It has been divided into a grid comprising 66 squares and, as of noon today, 52 of them, or 80 per cent in all, have been cleaned. The material being vacuumed is being stored in a holding pond on Dow's property.
My Department's scientific team posits that three possible factors have contributed to pollution problems in the St. Clair River. First, over the years there have "been spills from Dow and from other companies. Second, there is continuous discharge from the property of various companies directly into the river itself. Third, there is a continuous leakage, not from direct sources, that is to say from the companies themselves directly into the river, but from past underground waste disposal practices.
In my few remaining remarks I will address the third theory, a theory which has received wide attention. It holds that industrial wastes injected into the salt caverns at a depth of 600 metres have seeped through crevices up into the river bed. That particular doomsday scenario, my experts tell me, is an extremely unlikely possibility. They are, therefore, concentrating their efforts elsewhere. The question of seepage from the Detroit Formation has not been answered, either positively or negatively, to date. There is no absolute certainty yet, but there is increasing evidence that the dominant cause of the problem is Dow's recent spill, combined with a degree of continuing seepage from various sources, plus past environmental accidents.
I can assure Members of the House, in conclusion, that my Department is taking strong measures to counter pollution of the kind that has concerned us in the St. Clair River. However, the steps now being formulated for action in 1986 will go far beyond the one situation, the St. Clair River, however serious.
First, my Department is drawing up plans to control chemicals from the cradle to the grave and even before, using birth control on some new chemicals, if you will. This action will take the form of tough screening to ensure that only safe compounds and safe uses are permitted.
Second, the Department has already begun a thorough review of all existing environmental legislation, in particular the Environmental Contaminants Act, with an eye to overhauling and strengthening the entire range of laws and regulations.
Statements by Ministers
This process will be completed in co-operation with the other federal and provincial Departments which share jurisdiction for pollution control.
Third, in connection with the aforementioned review, we are laying the groundwork for a major rationalization of environmental law within federal jurisdiction.
Finally, there is a need to be concerned, not only with pollutants, but also with the resources they damage. In that regard my Department is drawing up plans for a Canada-wide water policy, a need which was clearly enunciated in the recently released Pearse Report.
Despite these bold measures, no Government, no company, no individual can be complacent about the events which have occurred in the St. Clair River. However, 1 think that these events have been highly instructive for all Canadians concerned about environmental protection. The St. Clair is an index of the degree to which we have become a chemical society. What is more, the state of the river is an indictment of our society for its carelessness and shortsightedness. If we are committed to a new era of chemical care and control-and 1 can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the Government is unequivocally committed to that era and to bringing it about-the country must do an awful lot more than it has done to cope with what I have called the chemical society. If we take the actions required, the St. Clair River will be seen in future years to have been a turning point-yes, a watershed, quite literally-in the country's history.

Mr. Speaker, certainly it is not very helpful to receive a copy of the Minister's statement five minutes after he has started reading his text. It shows vacillation, it shows indecision until the last minute, and perhaps it shows a sloppy and disorganized office which cannot come up with a text in time for the Opposition to see it, even at the beginning of the Minister's statement. That process leaves very much to be desired, and my Leader has already made an intervention to that effect. It does not seem to be an isolated case. It seems to be an alarming and increasing pattern on the part of the so-called Progressive Conservative Government.
However, what disturbs me in the approach of the Minister is the fact that he made a high-sounding declaration about a chemical society and the St. Clair River perhaps being a turning point in the treatment of the situation in those waters. He did not address the broader and basic questions which flow from the cuts which he and his Government allowed in the research of toxic chemicals at a time when we badly need them. I am referring to the badly needed scientific knowledge, as corroborated two weeks ago by the Royal Society of Canada in its study, about the effect of toxic chemicals on human health and the cancellation of the centre which was announced in November, 1984 by the Conservative Government.
In addition to that, I refer to the cancellation of the $2.5 million which the Department of the Environment usually and regularly sought from the Treasury Board every year before

December 19, 1985
Statements by Ministers
April 1, in order to intensify and conduct research on the leaking of toxic chemical dump sites into the Niagara River. Of course I am referring, in larger terms, to the broad $70 million cut in the National Research Council which includes matters related to chemicals and substances affecting human health.
In his statement the Minister focused upon the St. Clair River, but he failed to address the broader question of our international obligations to the Americans under the Great Lakes Water Agreement. That is a very serious flaw in his presentation today. We have an obligation under that agreement to the Amercains. We have an obligation to the communities downstream to Sarnia and Windsor and to our native people on Walpole Island. We have an obligation to deliver on the Canadian side of the river because we want the Americans to respect their obligations along the Niagara River where millions of Americans and Canadians are affected by a similar situation. It is only that the chemicals are different.

It is the linkage, the overview and the understanding of the totality of the picture in the Minister's statement today that dismay and shock me. The Minister arrived today a few minutes after three o'clock, apologized and expected to be treated in a kind manner both on substance as well as on process. That, Mr. Speaker, we cannot do for him.
Second, there has been a failure on the part of the Minister to recognize that the problem is not that of having a chemical society. We can have a chemical society with the number of chemical products that are produced and still have a clean society. The Minister has not addressed that point, the major point which preoccupies everyone in the country. Responsible companies and institutions can produce chemical products and still ensure that our water and air remain clean.
In his statement, the Minister failed to address the number of incentives that already exist in the Income Tax Act which favour the corporations operating along the St. Clair River. He has not indicated whether or not he has incentives in mind for those same corporations, incentives which would encourage them to introduce along the St. Clair River the necessary works that will permit the companies to clean up their acts at an accelerated pace.
Everyone knows that there are some companies along the St. Clair River which, in their daily operations, do discharge into the St. Clair River without sewer separation. This is a situation that must be remedied. Therefore, it is necessary to focus on the instruments the Government of Canada has in the Income Tax Act to accelerate the initiatives of companies toward cleaning up their daily operations now. If the facilities that exist in the Income Tax Act are not adequate for this purpose, perhaps the Minister could indicate which incentives he1 would like to adopt in order for the, companies to separate the sewage, treat the discharges so that they will not be released into the river until they are safe and ensure that the
monitoring equipment is up to date and not just mechanical as is the case with some of these corporations.
As the Minister said, the report is incomplete and I agree with that. It is a report that is based on temporary information. It does not really go to the cause of the problem. It simply deals with an assessment of the situation and its manifestations about which we know already. We have here a dangerous situation. Dow Chemical alone experienced some 11 spills between January and August of this year. Evidently, it is a company that has had certain difficulties and certain operating shortcomings that must be addressed.
The Minister has not addressed the shortcomings in the day-to-day operations of the companies that are causing the problem, willingly or unwillingly. In true Tory fashion, he has dealt with the symptoms and not with the root of the problem. That is what is distressing about his statement. He has simply told us to accept the fact that we have a chemical society and that we are now examining this particular river. He said in beautiful words that he was unequivocally committed to a new era but how are we going to arrive at a new era? That is what we want to know. I would have hoped that the Minister would have shown some leadership in coming to the House today before Christmas to indicate to us the road that he intends to travel beyond expressions of good intentions. That is not good enough.
We would like to express our dismay with the handling of this matter so far and also with another matter. At this time, two months have gone by since the Americans have submitted to the Government of Canada a plan regarding another river but one which is linked with this one because of our international obligations. The plan involves how to deal with the leaching along the Niagara River, a plan to which the Minister has not yet responded. The Government has not said a word about it. Therefore, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House do now adjourn.
